Dual-fuel strategies offer a range of flexibility specific combustion strategies and amounts of diesel displacement. Spark ignition technologies would require a more substantial retrofit, including redesigning the cylinder head to account for the spark system, optimizing the in-cylinder combustion geometry, compression ratio, and cylinder flow characteristics to best match the fuel for highest efficiency and lowest possible emissions. Spark ignition engines with low-cetane (high-octane) fuels are traditionally not used in high-torque applications such as line-haul locomotives, because engine knock at high loads can damage the engine and severely impact its useful lifespan. Very high-octane fuels like natural gas are often used with spark ignition or pre-chamber spark ignition system for stationary power. However, most commercial implementations for heavy-duty and rail have used diesel ignition dual-fuel engines that mitigate the end-gas autoignition knock behavior seen in spark ignition systems. Figure 2-11 summarizes the retrofit applications for the alternative fuels studied in this project. These alternatives have a wide range of properties that dictate how well suited they are for use as diesel fuel replacements, what additional storage and fuel delivery considerations are needed, and whether a secondary ignition source is needed. Bio-oils have moderate cetane numbers, which is a measure of how easily fuel will auto-ignite in diesel engines; higher cetane numbers are better. The efficiency and emissions for the near-drop-in replacements of BD and RD are the most well understood, and for this project are taken from GREET. Many alternative fuels lack efficiency data and emissions factors for the engines specific to this sector. Additional R&D is needed to understand the maximum diesel replacement for dual-fuel operation with low-cetane alternative fuels such as ethanol, methanol, and ammonia, and the use of bio-oils as a diesel replacement. Ethanol, methanol, and ammonia have low cetane ratings (or high octane, which is a measure of fuel’s resistance to knocking during combustion). These fuels higher octane rating will have trouble in compression ignition engines. A solution to this is using these fuels along with pilot fuel in a dual fuel engine. Previous dual-fuel research has assessed dual-fuel natural-gas/diesel solutions for locomotive four- stroke engines. For example, Klingbeil et al. (2020) showed that dual-fuel engines are somewhat 22 less efficient than the diesel-fuel baseline for simple retrofits and potential replacement limits below 60%, but that better than 90% replacement and diesel-like efficiency was possible with additional engineering. For these fuel solutions to be used in the North American market, they must meet the same emissions standards as the current diesel engine fleet.
